text: The hilltop church above Marseilles harbour. Its height made it the port's lookout post, from which approaching ships were signalled to the town.
quote: the look-out at Notre-Dame de la Garde

text: The officer on a merchant ship in charge of the cargo, its buying and selling, and the accounts: the owner's business agent at sea, not a navigator.
quote: here is your supercargo, M. Danglars

text: An old catch-all diagnosis for a sudden high fever with delirium. Today it might be called meningitis or encephalitis.
quote: he died of brain-fever in dreadful agony

text: A sailor who died on a voyage was sewn into his hammock or a canvas sack, weighted with cannon shot so that it would sink, and lowered into the sea after prayers.
quote: sewn up in his hammock with a thirty-six-pound shot

text: The Legion of Honour, France's highest decoration, created by Napoleon in 1802. Leclere won his through long service, the 'ten years' of war against Britain under the Revolution and Empire.
quote: his sword and cross of honor

text: France's basic currency. In 1815 a labourer might earn one or two francs a day, so 25,000 francs, the profit on a single voyage, was a very large sum.
quote: not to take 25,000 francs for the profits

text: A small island off the coast of Tuscany. Napoleon abdicated in April 1814 and was given Elba to rule in exile. In February 1815 he was living there, a few days' sail from France.
quote: a day and a half at the Island of Elba

text: Portoferraio, the chief port and town of Elba, where Napoleon and his small court lived.
quote: his landing at Porto-Ferrajo

text: Mild French oaths. 'Pardieu' means 'by God!'; 'peste', literally 'plague!', is more like 'good heavens!'
quote: Pardieu! and that is true!

text: Marseilles was founded around 600 BC by Greek colonists from Phocaea in Asia Minor, so its people are poetically called Phocaeans. La Canebière is its proud main street, running down to the harbour.
quote: the modern Phocéens are so proud

text: A gold coin worth 20 francs. A hundred louis, or 2,000 francs a year, was handsome pay for a young captain, and many times a labourer's earnings.
quote: a captain at twenty, with a hundred louis pay

text: Sixty francs for three months comes to about two-thirds of a franc a day: barely enough for bread. That is why the cupboards are empty.
quote: you have lived for three months on sixty francs

text: Sailors routinely brought in a little contraband for themselves. Tobacco was a heavily taxed state monopoly in France, and coffee carried high duties, so neither was thought of as a real crime.
quote: some smuggled coffee and most capital tobacco

text: French: 'my faith!', meaning 'upon my word!' or 'well, really!'
quote: “Ma foi! it will be as well if he is not,”

text: The French feminine of 'Catalan': a Catalan woman, here Mercédès.
quote: is he still in love with the Catalane?

text: 'Père' ('Father') was a familiar title for an older tradesman, here the keeper of La Réserve, a tavern by the harbour. It does not mean he is a priest.
quote: Père Pamphile had seen Dantès pass

text: Spanish: an inn. The Catalans' houses are whitewashed inside like a Spanish inn.
quote: coated with whitewash, like a Spanish posada

text: The language of Provence. It is a Romance language distinct from French, and in 1815 it was the everyday speech of most people in Marseilles.
quote: One of its chiefs, who understood Provençal

text: The Venus of Arles, a Roman marble statue found at Arles in 1651 and now in the Louvre. It was a classic standard of female beauty.
quote: modelled after those of the Arlesian Venus

text: Close-knit communities like the Catalans expected their young people to marry within the group, and marriage between cousins was common. Mercédès points out that this is a custom, not a law.
quote: it is among the Catalans a sacred law to intermarry

text: Napoleonic France drafted young men by annual levy. Even with peace restored, Fernand is on the rolls and could be called up at any time.
quote: You are included in the conscription

text: A short stabbing dagger of the kind sailors carried.
quote: cross your Catalan knife with his dirk

text: Spanish banderilleros: the bullfighters who plant barbed darts in the bull's shoulders to goad it into charging.
quote: as the bull is by the bandilleros

text: Grand Marshal of the Palace, the head of Napoleon's household. Marshal Bertrand held the post and followed him to Elba.
quote: the letter which the grand marshal gave him

text: Christ's words in the Gospel of Matthew (7:7), which Danglars borrows to nudge Fernand.
quote: in the words of the gospel, seek, and you shall find

term: Tous les méchants sont buveurs d’eau
text: French drinking song: 'All wicked men drink water; the Flood proves it.' Caderousse uses it to excuse his drinking.
quote: Tous les méchants sont buveurs d’eau

text: The procureur du roi was the state prosecutor for a district, responsible for criminal cases including political ones. A deputy (substitut) acted in his absence.
quote: denounce him to the king’s procureur

text: A supporter of Napoleon. Under the restored Bourbon king Louis XVIII, plotting for the exiled emperor was treason, and royalist officials were quick to suspect it.
quote: as a Bonapartist agent

text: Joachim Murat, Napoleon's brother-in-law and dashing cavalry marshal, made King of Naples in 1808 and still on that throne in 1815. A letter 'from Murat' suggests a plot reaching from Naples to Elba.
quote: has been intrusted by Murat with a letter

text: Royalists' name for Napoleon, implying that he had stolen the throne from the rightful Bourbon kings.
quote: a letter for the usurper

text: The bell tower of the old church of Notre-Dame des Accoules, a landmark of Marseilles' old quarter.
quote: go up into the belfry of the Accoules

term: the Mayor at the city hall
text: Since the Revolution a French marriage became legal only before the mayor at the town hall. Banns had to be published first and a waiting period observed. Morrel's influence, and a fee, let the couple skip the delay.
quote: We have purchased permission to waive the usual delay

text: Families with property drew up a marriage contract before a notary, fixing the bride's dowry and what each spouse brought. Dantès jokes that with nothing on either side, theirs was quick and cheap.
quote: the other formalities—the contract—the settlement?

text: After the Terror, flamboyant young Parisians (the Incroyables) paraded their extravagant clothes in the city's gardens. Old Dantès's finery is a generation out of date.
quote: one of the aged dandies of 1796

text: The echinus is the sea urchin; clovis are small clams. Together with the lobsters and prawns they make up the 'fruits of the sea' (fruits de mer).
quote: the echinus with its prickly outside

text: A sash worn by French magistrates and police commissaries as a sign of office when acting in the name of the law.
quote: a magistrate, wearing his official scarf

text: Napoleon gave up his throne in April 1814 after the allied armies took Paris. Regretting his fall, or serving the 'other government' as Morrel's uncle did, made a man politically suspect.
quote: regretting the abdication of Napoleon

text: The law courts of Marseilles, which housed the prosecutors' offices and connected to a holding prison.
quote: in the direction of the Palais de Justice

text: A royal military order founded by Louis XIV and revived at the Restoration. Its cross marked an officer loyal to the old monarchy.
quote: decorated with the cross of Saint Louis

text: Hartwell House in Buckinghamshire, England, where Louis XVIII lived in exile from 1809 until he took the throne in 1814.
quote: the patient exile of Hartwell

text: 1793–94, when the Revolutionary government guillotined thousands of suspected enemies, many of them nobles. Exiled nobles' lands were seized and sold off cheaply.
quote: for a mere trifle during the Reign of Terror

text: A member of the moderate republican faction of the Revolution. Many Girondins were themselves purged and guillotined by the radical Jacobins in 1793. Some had voted for Louis XVI's execution, which is why Villefort says his father did not.
quote: the son of a Girondin

term: the 9th Thermidor and the 4th of April
text: 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794, by the Revolutionary calendar) was the day Robespierre fell, ending the Terror. Early April 1814 saw Napoleon forced to abdicate. Royalists celebrated both dates.
quote: the 9th Thermidor and the 4th of April

text: Two Paris squares. The Place Louis XV (now the Place de la Concorde) held the guillotine that executed Louis XVI and later Robespierre. In the Place Vendôme stands a bronze column, cast from captured cannon, that celebrates Napoleon's victories.
quote: his scaffold in the Place Louis Quinze

text: When the army was cut back in 1814, thousands of Napoleon's officers were put on half pay. Idle, poor and resentful, they were a natural pool of Bonapartist feeling.
quote: Marseilles is filled with half-pay officers

text: A pact of Russia, Austria and Prussia, formally signed only in September 1815, so Dumas uses the name loosely for the victorious allies. Saint Helena, where they talk of sending Napoleon, is a tiny British island in the remote South Atlantic.
quote: the Holy Alliance purpose removing him from thence

text: An old measure of distance, about 4 km (2.5 miles). Two thousand leagues is roughly 8,000 km.
quote: at least two thousand leagues from here

text: Latin, from Cicero: 'let arms yield to the toga', meaning that civil authority should rule over the military. Villefort means that the magistrate's robe now counts for more than the soldier's sword.
quote: “Cedant arma togæ,” said Villefort with a bow.

text: The commissaire de police, the local police official who made arrests and gathered evidence for the prosecutor.
quote: he met the commissary of police

text: A crown (écu) is reckoned here at three francs, so Renée's dowry is about 150,000 francs, with half a million more to come. Either sum was a fortune when a labourer earned a franc or two a day.
quote: The dowry of his wife amounted to fifty thousand crowns

text: Saint Paul's phrase (2 Corinthians 12:2) for the highest heaven, used here to mean the height of bliss.
quote: recalled Villefort from the third heaven to earth

text: Secret revolutionary societies that began in the Kingdom of Naples (the name means 'charcoal burners'). To a royalist the word stood for any conspiracy.
quote: a member of some Carbonari society

text: France's armed military police, used for arrests, escorts and guarding prisoners.
quote: full of police agents and gendarmes

text: The juge d'instruction, or examining magistrate, who formally investigated a case before any trial. Villefort claims he must consult him.
quote: I must consult the trial justice

text: The Frioul islands off Marseilles (Pomègue, Ratonneau and the little Île d'If) and the waters around them, just outside the harbour mouth.
quote: they were, as Dantès knew, in the Frioul

term: like a Tuscan … like a Castilian
text: Tuscan Italian and Castilian Spanish were the prestige forms of each language, so Dantès speaks both like a well-spoken native.
quote: He spoke Italian like a Tuscan, and Spanish like a Castilian

text: A sou was a twentieth of a franc, so ten sous is half a franc a day, the allowance the jailer draws for each prisoner.
quote: every prisoner is worth ten sous a day

text: The jailer works out a hundred crowns as three hundred francs, a big bribe but small beside his post, worth 2,000 francs a year.
quote: I will give you a hundred crowns

text: The courtesy title of a French secular cleric, often a scholar or tutor rather than a parish priest. It does not mean the abbot of a monastery.
quote: that an abbé became mad

text: Lucius Junius Brutus, legendary founder of the Roman Republic, who sentenced his own sons to death for plotting to bring back the kings. He became a byword for stern duty.
quote: Guardian of the State, Royalist, Brutus

text: A royalist nickname for Napoleon, who was born in Corsica in 1769. It comes from propaganda that showed him as a monster devouring France's young men.
quote: Has the Corsican ogre broken loose?

text: French government bonds (rentes), traded on the Paris Bourse. Their price swung with political news, so selling 'at the market price' before bad news broke would save a fortune.
quote: All my fortune is in the funds

text: The Garde des Sceaux, France's minister of justice, who outranked every prosecutor and had the right to see the king at any hour.
quote: address yourself to the keeper of the seals

text: From Book 4 of Virgil's Aeneid: the deer that runs on with the hunter's arrow still in its side, an image for a wound that cannot be escaped.
quote: like Virgil’s wounded hero, he carried the arrow

text: Riders who guided post-horses. Changing to fresh horses at relay stations every few leagues let a traveller cross France fast, and quicker still for extra fees.
quote: ordering the postilions to drive

text: E. T. A. Hoffmann (1776–1822), German author of eerie, fantastical tales, said to have written fuelled by punch.
quote: spectres such as Hoffmann strews over his punch-drenched pages

text: The royal palace in Paris beside the Louvre, the seat of government for Napoleon and the Bourbons alike. It burned in 1871.
quote: enter at the Tuileries the little room

text: King of the French from 1830 to 1848, and on the throne when Dumas wrote the novel in 1844. Dumas is reminding readers that the same study served three rulers.
quote: and now of Louis Philippe

term: the seven fat kine and the seven lean kine
text: Pharaoh's dream in Genesis 41, which Joseph explains as seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. 'Kine' is an old plural of 'cow'.
quote: the seven fat kine and the seven lean kine

text: Latin: 'we sing to the deaf'. The king is saying that warnings would fall on deaf ears.
quote: “Canimus surdis,” replied the king

text: The opening words of Horace's Odes 1.15: 'When the shepherd [Paris] was carrying off [Helen]'. In this ode the sea god Nereus warns Paris of the war his crime will bring. 'Mala ducis avi domum' ('with evil omen you lead her home') and 'molli fugiens anhelitu' ('fleeing, softly panting') come from the same poem.
quote: a delightful note on the Pastor quum traheret

text: Latin, from Virgil's Aeneid (6.86): 'wars, terrible wars', the Sibyl's prophecy to Aeneas.
quote: bella, horrida bella

text: Two of Napoleon's most famous victories, over the Austrians in 1800 and the Austrians and Russians in 1805.
quote: as if he had gained another Marengo or Austerlitz

text: In Virgil's Eclogues, pairs of shepherds compete in song by answering each other verse for verse, just as the king and his minister take turns here.
quote: spoke alternately, like Virgil’s shepherds

text: The Chappe optical telegraph: a chain of hilltop towers whose movable arms relayed coded signals. It could carry a message across France in hours, but only in daylight and clear weather.
quote: we have a telegraph which transmits messages in three or four hours

text: Latin, from Horace (Odes 3.3): 'the man who is just and firm of purpose'. 'Tenax', the motto the king jokingly offers Blacas, means 'tenacious'.
quote: “Justum et tenacem propositi virum.”

text: Golfe-Juan, a bay near Antibes on the Riviera, where Napoleon came ashore on 1 March 1815. He then took the mountain road north through Gap and Sisteron, still known as the Route Napoléon.
quote: near Antibes, in the Gulf of Juan

text: The coalition of European powers, including Russia, Prussia, Austria and Britain, that defeated Napoleon in 1813–14 and put Louis XVIII on the throne after his 25 years in exile.
quote: seven conjoined and allied armies overthrew that man

text: A famous jibe at the Bourbons and their returning émigrés, usually credited to Talleyrand. It meant that exile had taught them nothing, and that they had forgotten none of their old privileges or grudges.
quote: We have learnt nothing, forgotten nothing!

term: the scaffold of my brother, Louis XVI.
text: Louis XVIII's elder brother, King Louis XVI, was guillotined by the Revolution in January 1793.
quote: mount the scaffold of my brother, Louis XVI.

text: A million and a half francs a year for spies and informers, an enormous budget at a time when a skilled worker might earn under a thousand francs a year.
quote: fifteen hundred thousand francs for secret service money

term: officer of the Legion of Honor
text: The Legion has grades. A knight (chevalier) wears a plain red ribbon, while an officer wears a rosette and a cross of higher rank, more than a young provincial magistrate could expect. A brevet is the official certificate of the award.
quote: this is an officer’s cross

text: A horse-drawn cab for hire, the taxi of its day.
quote: looking about him for a hackney-coach

text: The Montagnards ('the Mountain'), the radical Jacobin deputies who sat on the high benches of the Revolutionary assembly. In 1793 they drove out and hunted down the Girondins.
quote: proscribed by the mountaineers

term: the sin which ruined our first parents
text: Curiosity: Eve and Adam ate the forbidden fruit of knowledge in Genesis. Germain has been listening at the door.
quote: the sin which ruined our first parents

text: The return of the Bourbon kings in 1814, when Louis XVIII came back after Napoleon's fall.
quote: will the Restoration adopt imperial methods so promptly?

text: The toll gates in the wall around Paris, where goods were taxed and travellers could be watched.
quote: half an hour after you had passed the barrier

text: This echoes a famous, probably invented, joke about Paris newspapers in March 1815. Their headlines supposedly grew more respectful each day as Napoleon came nearer, from 'the monster has landed' to 'His Majesty has entered Paris'.
quote: you call the Corsican ogre, who at Nevers is styled the usurper

text: Napoleon's regiments carried standards topped with gilded eagles. His proclamation on landing promised that 'the eagle' would fly from steeple to steeple all the way to Notre-Dame.
quote: as rapidly as his own eagles

text: Louis IX (reigned 1226–70) was made a saint, and the Bourbon kings proudly claimed descent from him.
quote: a grandson of Saint Louis

text: A battle in northern Italy in 1796, famous for the young General Bonaparte leading a charge across a bridge under fire, flag in hand.
quote: the man of Arcola, Marengo, Austerlitz

text: Napoleon's brief return to power in 1815, from his arrival in Paris on 20 March until his final abdication in late June, roughly a hundred days.
quote: Twice during the Hundred Days had Morrel renewed his demand

text: The battle in Belgium on 18 June 1815 where Wellington and Blücher defeated Napoleon. It ended the Hundred Days, and Louis XVIII returned to the throne in July (the 'second restoration').
quote: At last there was Waterloo

text: Fortress prisons for state prisoners: two in the Piedmontese Alps and one on an island off Cannes. Pignerol and Sainte-Marguerite famously held the 'Man in the Iron Mask'.
quote: taken to Fenestrelles, to Pignerol, or to the Sainte-Marguérite islands

term: since the reign of Louis XIV.
text: Under the old monarchy a sealed royal order, the lettre de cachet, could lock someone up indefinitely without trial. Villefort suggests that such 'disappearances' never really stopped.
quote: since the reign of Louis XIV.

text: The government-appointed head of a département, one of France's administrative regions, with charge of police and prisons.
quote: the governors of the prison or the prefect of the department

text: After Waterloo, royalist mobs in Provence and Languedoc attacked and murdered suspected Bonapartists, the so-called White Terror of 1815. Helping the family of a 'Bonapartist' took courage.
quote: the south was aflame

text: A senior official sent from Paris to tour prisons, check conditions and hear prisoners' complaints.
quote: a visit was made by the inspector-general of prisons

text: The great lunatic asylum just outside Paris.
quote: I made some curious observations on this at Charenton

text: The Greek mathematician, said to have been killed by a Roman soldier at the fall of Syracuse (212 BC) while absorbed in drawing geometric figures.
quote: as Archimedes was when the soldier of Marcellus slew him

term: kingdom of Rome for his infant son
text: Napoleon annexed Rome to his empire and gave his son, born in 1811, the title 'King of Rome' at birth. Much of Italy was carved into French départements.
quote: the emperor had created the kingdom of Rome for his infant son

text: In The Prince (1513), the Florentine thinker Niccolò Machiavelli called for a strong ruler to unite and free Italy, and held up Cesare Borgia as a model.
quote: the dream of Machiavelli and Cæsar Borgia

text: A biblical phrase (Psalm 115; Mark 8:18) for people who refuse to see what is in front of them.
quote: having eyes see not, and having ears hear not

text: Roman emperors notorious for wild extravagance. Nero once sent men digging in Africa for the legendary buried gold of Queen Dido.
quote: Caligula or Nero, those treasure-seekers

text: Convicts 'sent to the galleys' by then served hard labour at the naval prisons of Toulon or Brest. They were branded, dressed in red, and chained in pairs, but they worked in the open air.
quote: the infamous costume, the chain, and the brand

text: John Martin (1789–1854), English painter of vast, apocalyptic scenes of ancient cities, such as Belshazzar's Feast and The Fall of Babylon.
quote: in Martin’s Babylonian pictures

text: In Dante's Inferno (cantos 32–33), Count Ugolino was starved to death in a tower with his sons. In hell he gnaws forever at the skull of Archbishop Ruggieri, who betrayed him.
quote: as the implacable Ugolino devours the skull of Archbishop Roger

text: The 'writing on the wall' in Daniel 5. A ghostly hand writes these words at King Belshazzar's feast, foretelling his downfall.
quote: the mene, mene, tekel upharsin of Belshazzar

text: In Greek myth, Tantalus was punished in the underworld by standing in water beneath fruit trees, with food and drink always just out of reach. Dantès is a 'voluntary' one because he refuses his own food.
quote: like a voluntary Tantalus, he refused himself

term: where two or three are gathered together
text: Christ's promise in Matthew 18:20: 'where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.'
quote: prayers where two or three are gathered together

text: Faria compares France with England. There, Charles I was executed (1649), Cromwell ruled, the monarchy returned under Charles II, and James II was ousted in 1688 by his son-in-law William of Orange, stadtholder (head of state) of Holland. Parliament's rights then grew.
quote: After Charles I., Cromwell; after Cromwell, Charles II.

text: Two Renaissance popes with dreams of power in Italy. Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia, pope 1492–1503) was Cesare Borgia's father; Clement VII (Giulio de' Medici, pope 1523–34) belonged to the Florentine banking dynasty.
quote: It was the plan of Alexander VI. and Clement VII.

text: Famous jailbreaks. The Duc de Beaufort escaped the fortress of Vincennes in 1648, and Latude got out of the Bastille in 1756 down a rope ladder made from his linen.
quote: the escape of the Duc de Beaufort from the Château de Vincennes

text: Antoine Lavoisier, founder of modern chemistry, was guillotined in 1794. Pierre Cabanis (1757–1808) was a celebrated physician and philosopher.
quote: I know Lavoisier, and was the intimate friend of Cabanis

text: A large book size, made by folding each printed sheet twice to give four leaves.
quote: will make one large quarto volume

text: The less familiar names on Faria's list. Famiano Strada was a 17th-century Jesuit historian of the Dutch wars; Jordanes was a 6th-century historian of the Goths.
quote: Titus Livius, Tacitus, Strada, Jornandes

text: Catholic fast days ('lean' days) when meat was forbidden and fish was served instead. Faria names Wednesday, Friday and Saturday.
quote: served to us on maigre days

text: Gujarat in western India and Golconda near Hyderabad, whose legendary diamond mines and markets made 'Golconda' a byword for fabulous riches.
quote: the mines of Guzerat and Golconda

term: to whom … could be in any way advantageous
text: The old Roman legal question 'cui bono?' ('who benefits?'), a detective's first rule long before detective stories.
quote: seek first to discover the person to whom the perpetration

text: The livre was the old French money unit, replaced by the nearly equal franc in 1795. The civil list is the yearly sum granted to a monarch for his household. Faria's point is that 12,000 livres matters as much to a clerk as 12 million does to a king.
quote: these twelve thousand livres are his civil list

text: René Descartes pictured the universe as whirling vortices of matter pressing on one another, an image for the jostling of competing interests.
quote: as in Descartes’ theory of pressure and impulsion

text: Napoleon turned Tuscany into the short-lived Kingdom of Etruria (1801–07) for a branch of the Bourbons. Its queen, Maria Luisa of Spain, kept a court in Florence.
quote: at the court of the Queen of Etruria

text: Modern (spoken) Greek, as opposed to the ancient language.
quote: a little of the Romaic dialect

text: A seizure in which the body goes rigid and seems lifeless. Faria's 'attacks', with convulsions and later paralysis, sound to modern ears like epilepsy and strokes.
quote: I am about to be seized with a fit of catalepsy

text: Blackletter, the heavy, angular script used in late-medieval manuscripts.
quote: traces of Gothic characters

text: A region of north-eastern Italy, nominally papal, which Cesare Borgia conquered in 1499–1503 with French backing from King Louis XII.
quote: The great wars of Romagna had ended

text: A cardinal's red hat is the symbol of his rank. Selling church offices (simony) was a notorious scandal of the Borgia papacy.
quote: he had the two hats to sell besides

text: Latin 'from the side': a papal envoy sent as the pope's personal representative, as if from his own side.
quote: it was a legate à latere

text: The book of daily prayers, psalms and readings that every priest was bound to recite.
quote: my breviary with the gold corners

text: Handing over capital in exchange for a fixed income for life. It raises your income, but nothing is left to your heirs.
quote: I advised him to invest all he had in an annuity

text: The Thousand and One Nights, the great collection of Middle Eastern tales, full of genies guarding treasure in caves. It was hugely popular in Europe from the 1700s.
quote: like the treasures of the Arabian Nights

text: Invisible ink that shows only when heated or treated, made from lemon juice, for example.
quote: traced in mysterious and sympathetic ink

text: The Roman crown (scudo) was a papal silver coin. Faria's 'thirteen millions' in francs was an almost unimaginable fortune when a comfortable family could live on a few thousand francs a year.
quote: Two millions of Roman crowns; nearly thirteen millions of our money

text: A legal arrangement that keeps family property intact and unsellable from generation to generation, so heirs may be 'rich' in jewels they cannot touch.
quote: handed down by entail, and which they cannot touch

text: A low, flat island south-west of Elba in the Tuscan archipelago.
quote: situated twenty-five miles from Pianosa

text: Latin: 'solid ground', dry land.
quote: which we take for terra firma

text: Like an electric shock. The word comes from Luigi Galvani, whose experiments made dead frogs' legs twitch with electricity.
quote: The draught produced a galvanic effect

text: A red-hot iron pressed to the heel was a standard way to confirm death. Fear of being buried alive was widespread in the period.
quote: “Let the irons be heated,” said the doctor

text: A fashionable 19th-century psychiatric diagnosis: madness on a single subject in someone otherwise sane.
quote: the sort of malady which we call monomania

text: The Catholic Mass for the dead.
quote: he might have had his requiem

text: France's method of execution from 1792. A capital crime committed in prison, such as killing a guard, would have led to it.
quote: then they will guillotine me

text: A flat frame with handles at each end, used for carrying a body.
quote: the noise they made in putting down the hand-bier

text: The cold, violent north-west wind that roars down the Rhône valley over Provence and out to sea.
quote: Dantès knew that the mistral was blowing

text: A lighthouse on a rocky islet south-west of Marseilles, which ships steered by.
quote: he saw the light of Planier

text: A tartan is a small Mediterranean coasting vessel with one main mast and a lateen sail, a large triangular sail on a long slanting yard. Craft like this were favoured by traders and smugglers.
quote: he knew it to be a Genoese tartan

term: a vow, to our Lady of the Grotto
text: Mediterranean sailors in peril often made vows to the Virgin Mary, such as leaving their hair and beard uncut for a set time, so Dantès's excuse sounds perfectly natural.
quote: I made a vow, to our Lady of the Grotto

text: The old English name for Livorno, Tuscany's busy free port and a hub of Mediterranean trade, legal and otherwise.
quote: “To Leghorn.”

text: A fathom is six feet (about 1.8 m), so twenty fathoms is about 36 metres: a close shave past the rocks.
quote: You shall pass it by twenty fathoms

text: The usual Mediterranean term for the master or skipper of a small trading vessel.
quote: said the patron

text: The old word for the left-hand (port) side of a ship, facing forward.
quote: “Larboard your helm,” cried the captain

text: A fortress fired a cannon to announce an escape, warning the coast and boats to watch for the fugitive.
quote: they are firing the alarm gun

text: The great Venetian painter (c. 1488–1576), whose portraits often show grave, full-bearded men.
quote: one of Titian’s portraits

text: Strictly, a small boat with four-cornered lugsails. Here it is used loosely for the tartan.
quote: handled the lugger

term: the country of Paoli and Napoleon
text: Corsica. Pasquale Paoli led the island's fight for independence from Genoa and France (1755–69), and Napoleon was born there.
quote: the country of Paoli and Napoleon

text: Culverins were small, long-barrelled cannon. Shallops were light open boats used for ferrying cargo to shore.
quote: mounted two small culverins

text: Tuscan lire, worth less than the franc. Eighty francs for one night's work was perhaps a labourer's wages for a month or two.
quote: a hundred Tuscan livres, or about eighty francs

term: Pain, thou art not an evil
text: Words of the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, who said this while racked by gout, as told by Cicero. The Stoics held that pain does not harm a man's virtue.
quote: “Pain, thou art not an evil.”

text: The relentlessly optimistic tutor in Voltaire's satire Candide (1759), who insists that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.
quote: Doctor Pangloss believed it

text: Large silver coins (Spanish dollars and their Italian equivalents) used across the Mediterranean, worth roughly five francs each. A hundred piastres is about 500 francs.
quote: he had amassed a hundred piastres

text: The Roman messenger god, patron of merchants, travellers and thieves alike, hence Dumas's joke about smugglers.
quote: Mercury, the god of merchants and robbers

text: The mixed trade language of Mediterranean ports, built from Italian, Spanish, French, Arabic and Greek.
quote: jumbled in a lingua franca

text: A knot is a speed of one nautical mile (about 1.85 km) per hour, so ten knots is brisk sailing for a small vessel. 'Knots an hour' is a common slip.
quote: They were making nearly ten knots an hour

text: In Livy, an oracle said the first man to kiss his mother would rule Rome. Lucius Brutus pretended to stumble and kissed the earth, the mother of all.
quote: like Lucius Brutus, have “kissed his mother earth.”

text: Mount Pelion in Greece. In myth, giants piled Pelion on Mount Ossa to storm heaven. Dumas is evoking a wild, rugged mountain.
quote: the rocky hills of this second Pelion

text: Montepulciano, a Tuscan red wine.
quote: a flask of Monte Pulciano

text: From an Indian title for a provincial governor. It came to mean Europeans who came home from India with vast fortunes and flaunted them.
quote: the insolence of nabobs

text: A nimble wild goat-antelope of the Alps, famous for leaping from rock to rock.
quote: with the boldness of a chamois

text: The magic password that opens the robbers' treasure cave in 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves'. Dumas confuses Ali Baba, a woodcutter, with the fisherman of another Arabian Nights tale.
quote: opened the splendid caverns of Ali Baba to the Arabian fisherman

text: The narrow channel between Corsica and Sardinia, about 11 km wide, notorious for strong winds and currents.
quote: just disappearing in the straits of Bonifacio

text: In Greek myth, Daedalus built the Labyrinth for King Minos, a maze so intricate that hardly anyone who entered could find the way out. So: a bewildering puzzle.
quote: the Dædalian labyrinth of probabilities

text: Potassium nitrate, the key ingredient of gunpowder. A cloth soaked in it burns slowly and steadily, so it makes a simple fuse.
quote: rolling his handkerchief in saltpetre

text: In Greek myth, the giant elder gods (and the Giants after them) who made war on Zeus, the 'father of the gods', tearing up mountains to storm heaven.
quote: he seemed like one of the ancient Titans

text: The Visigoth king who sacked Rome in 410. He was buried with his treasure in the bed of the Busento river, turned aside for the purpose, and legend says the captives who dug the grave were killed to keep the secret.
quote: those who buried Alaric, and were interred with the corpse

text: Foul-smelling and unhealthy to breathe; used of stale or poisonous air in caves, mines and sewers.
quote: the thick and mephitic atmosphere he had expected

text: French heraldic term: set upright down the centre of the shield. The cardinal's hat above the shield marks the arms of a churchman.
quote: a sword, en pale, on an oval shield

text: At Dumas's valuation of about 80 francs a coin, the coins alone come to some two million francs, when a labourer earned perhaps 500–600 francs a year. The gold bars and jewels are worth more still. Alexander VI was the Borgia pope (1492–1503).
quote: twenty-five thousand crowns, each worth about eighty francs

text: A large silver coin worth roughly 5 francs, used all round the Mediterranean (it began as the Spanish peso). Dumas also uses the word for the papal scudo.
quote: fifty piastres each

term: a Jew, a dealer in precious stones
text: Leghorn (Livorno) had one of Europe's largest Jewish communities, invited in by the Medici in the 1590s and prominent in the gem, coral and banking trades. Dumas's bare label 'a Jew' reflects the casual prejudice of his era.
quote: the house of a Jew, a dealer in precious stones

text: A certificate that a ship came from a port free of plague and other contagion. Port officials checked it before anyone could land; without it, a ship could be held in quarantine.
quote: to demand his bill of health

text: Passports were needed even for travel within France. A rich English 'milord' abroad was assumed to be wealthy and harmless, and had his government's protection, so officials usually waved him through with few questions.
quote: presented an English passport he had obtained from Leghorn

text: Marseilles's broad main street, running up from the Old Port. Its name comes from the hemp (Provençal canebe) once worked into rope there.
quote: as he landed on the Canebière

text: A 40-franc gold coin (a napoleon was 20 francs, the same as a louis). The sailor expected a 2-franc piece and was handed twenty times as much, which was probably several weeks' pay.
quote: you gave me a double Napoleon

text: From nawab, a governor in Mughal India. In Europe it meant a man who had come home with a huge fortune made in India and spent it lavishly.
quote: Some nabob from India

text: Large fishing nets that hang upright in the water, held up by floats and weighted at the bottom. A tender is a small boat that serves a larger one.
quote: two seines and a tender

text: Marseilles's northern gate, where the road leaves for Aix and the interior, the way to the Rhône valley.
quote: leave Marseilles by the Porte d’Aix

text: A Roman aqueduct bridge (1st century AD) with three tiers of arches over the river Gardon near Nîmes, one of the best-preserved Roman monuments in France. The inn's sign shows it.
quote: a grotesque representation of the Pont du Gard

text: A town on the Rhône whose great July fair drew merchants from all over Europe and the Mediterranean. It was one of the biggest trade fairs of its day, with jewellers, cloth dealers and bankers.
quote: between the town of Beaucaire and the village of Bellegarde

term: a canal between Beaucaire and Aiguemortes
text: The Beaucaire canal, finished in the early 19th century, linked the Rhône to the coast. Barges took over traffic from the road, ruining roadside inns like this one.
quote: a canal between Beaucaire and Aiguemortes had revolutionized transportation

text: Malarial fever, with recurring fits of shivering and chills. It was common around the marshes of the Camargue and Aigues-Mortes, which is the 'slow fever' wasting La Carconte.
quote: went into a fit of ague

text: A dark, strong red wine from the Lot valley in south-west France, sometimes called 'black wine'.
quote: one of the few bottles of Cahors still remaining

text: Rough, grainy leather made from horse hide or the skin of sharks and rays, often dyed and used to cover small cases.
quote: a small box covered with black shagreen

text: The bagne, the convict prison at Toulon naval port. Convicts were still said to be sent 'to the galleys', though by then they did chained hard labour in the dockyards rather than rowing ships.
quote: at the galleys of Toulon

text: Louis XVIII's return to the throne in July 1815, after Waterloo ended the Hundred Days. The first restoration was in 1814, after Napoleon's first abdication.
quote: released from prison during the second restoration

text: When a labourer earned perhaps 500–600 francs a year, this was a life-changing sum. Invested at 5%, it would bring in about 2,500 francs a year: a modest, comfortable income, though not riches.
quote: It was estimated at fifty thousand francs.

text: Someone who talks pious cant, i.e. a religious hypocrite. Caderousse's dislike of the Jesuits, a powerful Catholic order, reflects a common anticlerical feeling of the time.
quote: I, who am no canter, and hate the Jesuits

text: Two valuable dyes: cochineal, a crimson made from dried insects, and indigo, a deep blue made from a plant. Both were expensive imports and made a rich cargo.
quote: a cargo of cochineal and indigo

text: 16 June 1815: Napoleon's last victory, over the Prussians, two days before Waterloo. On the eve of the campaign the real General Bourmont went over to the enemy with his staff.
quote: was at the battle of Ligny

text: In 1823 France invaded Spain to restore the absolute power of King Ferdinand VII. The storming of the Trocadero fort at Cádiz ended the campaign. Supplying the army (the commissariat) made contractors rich.
quote: after the taking of Trocadero, he was made colonel

text: Trading in government bonds (rentes) on the Paris Bourse. Their prices rose and fell with war and political news, a quick road to riches or ruin for anyone with inside knowledge.
quote: he speculated in the funds

text: The lowest French noble title; a count ranks two steps higher. Napoleon and the restored Bourbons both gave out titles freely, and rich financiers were often made barons, to the scorn of the old nobility.
quote: now he is the Baron Danglars

text: The Greeks' revolt against Ottoman Turkish rule (1821–1829). Supporting Greece was a Romantic fashion across Europe, and Lord Byron died there in 1824 as a volunteer.
quote: Greece only had risen against Turkey

text: Hamlet's bitter line (Act 1, scene 2) about his mother's hasty remarriage after his father's death.
quote: ‘Frailty, thy name is woman.’

text: A smart street in Paris just off the Boulevard des Italiens, in the fashionable new quarter of bankers, officers and society people.
quote: No. 27, Rue du Helder, Paris

text: A louis was a 20-franc gold coin, so this purse held 500 francs. That is five times what Fernand sent by his valet, and close to a year's wages for a labourer.
quote: it contained five-and-twenty louis

text: A sturdy yellowish cotton cloth, originally from Nanjing in China, popular for summer trousers.
quote: nankeen trousers, and a white waistcoat

text: Under French commercial law, a merchant who failed to pay a bill on its due date could be declared bankrupt (en faillite). That meant public disgrace, loss of civic rights and exclusion from the Bourse until every creditor was paid.
quote: It looks more like bankruptcy!

text: Money or property a bride's family brought to her marriage. In respectable families a match was hard to make without one, and losing it could end an engagement.
quote: were the dowry of my daughter

text: A fee for arranging a financial deal, normally a small percentage. Boville expects to sell his doubtful debt at a heavy discount, but the Englishman pays the full face value and asks for a favour instead of a fee.
quote: I only ask a brokerage.

text: Guns were named by the weight of shot they fired. A 36-pounder ball weighs about 16 kg, more than enough to drag a body straight to the bottom.
quote: after fastening a thirty-six-pound cannon-ball to their feet

text: 'The White Flag', an ultra-royalist Paris newspaper named after the Bourbon white flag, the opposite of Napoleon's tricolour. It was fitting reading for an official of the restored monarchy.
quote: was reading Le Drapeau Blanc

term: at the end of his teeth
text: A literal rendering of the French rire du bout des dents: to laugh only with the teeth, i.e. a forced, mirthless laugh.
quote: he laughed as the English do, “at the end of his teeth.”

text: Hero of a cycle of tales in the Arabian Nights: a Baghdad merchant who made seven fabulous voyages, survived shipwrecks, giants and monsters, and came home richer each time.
quote: a letter signed ‘Sinbad the Sailor.’

text: The clerks' nickname echoes Horatius Cocles, the legendary one-eyed Roman who held a bridge alone against an invading army. In Latin, cocles means 'one-eyed'.
quote: an old one-eyed cashier, called “Cocles,”

text: A sou was 5 centimes, so twenty made a franc and fourteen sous is 70 centimes, perhaps a third of a day's pay. Cocles accounts for every last coin.
quote: an overbalance of fourteen sous in his cash

text: A lookout room or turret on a rooftop, built for the view. From Morrel's, it looks out over the harbour.
quote: passes a part of his time in a belvedere

text: Bills of exchange were signed promises to pay a sum on a fixed date. They could be signed over ('assigned') to someone else, so a merchant's debts could be quietly bought up and presented by a stranger.
quote: assigned to our house by the holders

text: A huge sum: a labourer on 500–600 francs a year would need centuries to earn it. For a merchant with his credit gone, there is no hope of raising it quickly.
quote: in all, 287,500 francs

text: Headlands on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa (in today's Mauritania and Western Sahara). They lie on the long route home from India around the Cape of Good Hope.
quote: between Cape Blanc and Cape Boyador

text: To reef is to shorten a sail by tying part of it up, so the wind has less to push on. Studding-sails and the flying jib are light extra sails. 'Scudding under bare poles' means running before a storm with no sail set at all.
quote: Take in two reefs in the top-sails

text: A wad of chewing tobacco, kept in the cheek.
quote: Penelon rolled his quid in his cheek

text: A roll of coins wrapped in paper, here a hundred francs' worth in each hand.
quote: a rouleau of a hundred francs in either hand

text: When a bill went unpaid, a notary formally recorded the refusal. This 'protest' was a public step toward a declaration of bankruptcy.
quote: the bills would go to protest at the end of the month

text: The École Polytechnique in Paris, founded in 1794: a highly competitive state college training engineers and artillery and military officers.
quote: passed brilliantly through the Polytechnic School

text: The Stoics, Greek and Roman philosophers, taught that a wise man does his duty and bears pain and misfortune without complaint. Hence the modern sense of 'stoic'.
quote: he thus gained the name of “the stoic.”

text: Marseilles was founded around 600 BC by Greeks from Phocaea in Asia Minor, so its citizens were called Phocaeans. The Sémaphore was the city's commercial newspaper, which listed ship movements.
quote: take his coffee at the club of the Phocéens

text: Paper bearing an official tax stamp, required by law for wills, contracts and other legal documents. That is why the sight frightens Madame Morrel.
quote: her husband was writing on stamped paper

text: A writing desk with drawers and a fold-down writing flap, usually lockable. It was where wills, money and private papers were kept.
quote: You will find my will in the secretaire in my bedroom.

text: Bankruptcy disgraced a merchant and his whole family. Some men of Morrel's class believed that dying rather than defaulting would save the family name, since people pitied a dead debtor where they shunned a living one.
quote: “Blood washes out dishonor,” said Morrel.

text: Fringed shoulder ornaments showing an officer's rank. By taking them off, Maximilian shows he will give up his army career to support his mother and sister.
quote: he took off his two epaulets, the insignia of his rank

text: Fort Saint-Jean, the medieval fortress guarding the north side of the entrance to Marseilles's Old Port.
quote: in front of the tower of Saint-Jean

text: The days of feasting and masquerade before Ash Wednesday and the Lenten fast. Rome's Carnival was the most famous in Europe, centred on the Corso with masks, flower-throwing and horse races, and it drew visitors from everywhere.
quote: They had agreed to see the Carnival at Rome that year

text: Italian: a guide who shows visitors the sights. The name jokingly compares these talkative guides to the orator Cicero.
quote: should act as cicerone to Albert

text: Ships that might have been in contact with disease, or with smugglers and pirates from suspect shores, were held in isolation before anyone could land. Mediterranean ports had enforced this strictly since the plague years.
quote: we shall have to perform quarantine for six days

text: Slang for killing a man. Gaetano is excusing the Corsican vendetta: by island custom, avenging a wrong to one's family was a duty, so the outlaws in Corsica's maquis were often feud-killers rather than robbers.
quote: they are pursued for having made a stiff

text: Italian: roughly 'make yourself at home'. Dumas compares it to the mock-Turkish word in Molière's comedy Le Bourgeois gentilhomme, which supposedly packs a whole speech into a few syllables.
quote: S’accommodi

text: Meyerbeer's grand opera Les Huguenots (1836) was a Paris sensation. Its hero, Raoul, is led blindfold to a secret meeting with a mysterious lady.
quote: those of Raoul in the Huguenots

text: The Thousand and One Nights, a collection of Middle Eastern tales hugely popular in Europe. Franz's jokes come from it: Ali Baba's treasure cave, opened by a magic word, and Aladdin with his wonderful lamp.
quote: the wonders of the Arabian Nights

text: A generous host. The usage comes from Molière's comedy Amphitryon: 'the true Amphitryon is the one who gives the dinner.'
quote: replied the singular Amphitryon

text: Hassan-i Sabbah (d. 1124), leader of the Nizari Ismaili sect that Europeans called the Assassins. Marco Polo's legend says he drugged followers to give them a taste of paradise. The word 'assassin' may come from hashishin, 'hashish-users'.
quote: of the Old Man of the Mountain

term: Monsieur Appert, and the man in the little blue cloak
text: Two well-known Paris philanthropists: Benjamin Appert, a campaigner for prison reform, and Edme Champion, nicknamed 'the little man in the blue cloak', who handed out food and clothing to the poor.
quote: rival Monsieur Appert, and the man in the little blue cloak

text: A burnous: a long hooded woollen cloak worn in North Africa.
quote: lying on his bournous in a bed of dry heather

text: A small port on a deep gulf on the south-east coast of Corsica, facing Sardinia.
quote: it disappeared in the gulf of Porto-Vecchio

text: Rome's great festivals: Carnival before Lent, Holy Week before Easter, Corpus Christi with its early-summer processions, and the feast of St Peter on 29 June, when St Peter's dome was lit up.
quote: at Rome there are four great events in every year

text: Horses kept at relay stations along the main roads, hired by stages to travellers and the mail. Pastrini says the few left are reserved for the official post.
quote: but can’t we have post-horses?

text: Dumas reckons Roman prices in lire, each worth roughly a franc. At 25–40 a day, hiring a carriage cost more than a labourer earned in a fortnight.
quote: one pays twenty-five lire for common days

text: The Via del Corso, Rome's long, straight main street, running from the Piazza del Popolo to the Piazza Venezia between rows of palaces. During Carnival its windows and balconies were rented out at enormous prices.
quote: In the Corso.

term: pulchinellos or shepherds of the Landes
text: Pulcinella is the hook-nosed clown of Italian comedy (the ancestor of Punch). The shepherds of the Landes, the marshy pine country of south-west France, herded their flocks on tall stilts, hence Albert's joke about seeing Carnival on stilts.
quote: monster pulchinellos or shepherds of the Landes

text: The fashionable Paris promenade now called the Boulevard des Italiens, nicknamed after Ghent, where Louis XVIII's courtiers waited out the Hundred Days. The Café de Paris was the city's most exclusive restaurant.
quote: their walk on the Boulevard de Gand, and the Café de Paris

text: Real brigand chiefs of the hills south of Rome. Antonio Gasbarrone terrorized the border between the Papal States and Naples until he surrendered in 1825. Harsh papal campaigns never managed to wipe out banditry.
quote: the Decesaris and the Gasparones were mere children

text: In Corneille's tragedy Horace (1640), old Horace is told his son fled from three enemies. Asked what the boy should have done, he answers 'Qu'il mourût!', 'He should have died!', a famous line of Roman sternness.
quote: worthy the ‘Let him die,’ of Corneille

text: Romantic outlaw heroes: Jean Sbogar, the gentleman-brigand of Charles Nodier's 1818 novel, and Lara, the mysterious, brooding chieftain of Byron's poem (1814).
quote: like Jean Sbogar or Lara

text: The sequin (zecchino) was a Venetian gold coin worth about 12 francs. Twenty a day is some 240 francs, nearly half a year's wages for a labourer, for one window.
quote: let to a Russian prince for twenty sequins a day

text: The papal scudo, worth about 5.4 francs, the same coin Dumas elsewhere calls a Roman piastre. Five hundred of them was a fortune to two orphaned farmhands.
quote: Five hundred Roman crowns are three thousand lire

text: French: a mild oath, roughly 'by Jove!', a softened par Dieu. Pardieu, morbleu, diable and peste ('plague!') are similar exclamations.
quote: Parbleu!

text: The Flavian Amphitheatre, opened in AD 80, where gladiators fought before some 50,000 spectators. Seeing its ruins by moonlight was an essential experience for Romantic-era travellers.
quote: show Albert the Colosseum by moonlight

text: Trastevere, the old working-class quarter 'across the Tiber'. Its people claimed to be the truest Romans and wore a distinctive costume.
quote: wore the Transtevere costume

text: The Emperor Hadrian's huge round tomb beside the Tiber, later turned into a papal fortress and prison.
quote: I came here direct from the Castle of St. Angelo

text: Italian: executed with a mallet (mazza), a punishment the Papal States reserved for the most savage murderers. Decapitato simply means beheaded.
quote: One of the culprits will be mazzolato

text: Donizetti's 1833 opera, based on Byron's poem: Duke Azzo learns that his wife Parisina loves Ugo when she murmurs her secret in her sleep. Donizetti also wrote Lucia di Lammermoor.
quote: The opera of Parisina was announced

text: The rank between baron and count, often used by a count's eldest son as a courtesy title. A title 'dated merely from 1815' was new nobility, unlike old families going back to the Middle Ages.
quote: he was a viscount—a recently created one, certainly

text: In Italian theatres a box was a private drawing room: people chatted, received visitors and listened to the opera only in snatches. A new visitor took the seat of honour and the earlier guest gave way.
quote: in obedience to the Italian custom, instantly rose

text: The pale, fascinating aristocrat-vampire of John Polidori's tale The Vampyre (1819). He was modelled on Byron, and the story was at first published as Byron's own. It was endlessly adapted on the Paris stage.
quote: no other than Lord Ruthven himself in a living form

text: A one-stringed bowed instrument from the Balkans, traditionally played to accompany sung epics.
quote: the sound of a guzla reached the ears

text: Italian (mannaia): the Papal States' version of the guillotine. Its crescent-shaped blade drops from a lower height than the French one.
quote: the curved knife of the mandaïa

text: Henri de Talleyrand, Comte de Chalais, was beheaded in 1626 for plotting against Cardinal Richelieu. His friends spirited the executioner away, and the untrained substitute needed some thirty strokes.
quote: the soldier who beheaded the Count of Chalais

text: Duels were illegal in France, but juries rarely convicted, and a gentleman who refused a challenge lost his honour. Insults among the upper classes were still settled with swords or pistols.
quote: it is to punish them that duelling is tolerated

text: The law of retaliation, found in the Bible (Exodus 21:24) and in older codes such as Hammurabi's. The count credits it to the peoples of the East.
quote: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth

term: torn to pieces by horses or broken on the wheel
text: Executions under the old French monarchy: quartering by horses for regicides, and the wheel, which broke the victim's limbs, for many murderers. In 1792 the Revolution replaced them with the guillotine, a quick death meant to be the same for everyone.
quote: torn to pieces by horses or broken on the wheel

text: Italian: 'At your convenience!' In other words, breakfast is served.
quote: Al suo commodo!

text: Edme-Samuel Castaing, a young Paris doctor guillotined in 1823 for poisoning a friend with morphine, after a sensational trial.
quote: I saw Castaing executed

text: Carnival confetti were not paper. They were small sugared sweets or, more often, cheap pellets of plaster and flour, flung by the handful at everyone in sight. Pale costumes hid the white dust.
quote: on account of the confetti (sweetmeats)

text: The great oval square inside Rome's northern gate, with an ancient Egyptian obelisk at its centre. It was the usual place for public executions, and the Corso runs from it.
quote: the spectacle that the Piazza del Popolo presented

text: Lay religious confraternities whose members wore hoods to stay anonymous. They comforted condemned prisoners, walked with them to the scaffold, and buried them.
quote: A brotherhood of penitents, clothed from head to foot

text: A loose hooded cloak, usually worn with a half-mask: the standard disguise at masked balls and carnivals.
quote: was a blue domino

text: A crowded etching by Jacques Callot (1635) showing the hermit saint besieged by swarms of grotesque demons.
quote: as in Callot’s Temptation of St. Anthony

text: A popular Paris farce by Eugène Scribe (1820) in which a man is dressed up in a bear's skin. Odry was its star comic actor.
quote: exactly resembling Odry’s in The Bear and the Pasha

text: A light carriage with a folding hood.
quote: that calash filled with Roman peasants

text: James de Rothschild, head of the family bank in Paris and reputedly the richest man in France: a byword for wealth.
quote: being confounded with M. de Rothschild

text: A small papal copper coin, a hundredth of a scudo. 'Not a bajocco' means not a penny.
quote: It does not bring him a bajocco.

text: Brooding heroes of Romantic drama: Didier in Victor Hugo's Marion de Lorme and Antony in Dumas's own play Antony (both 1831). Dumas is slyly quoting himself.
quote: two or three exits worthy of Didier or Anthony

text: Pope from 1831 to 1846, head of the Church and also ruler of the Papal States. He was a firm conservative, famously suspicious of railways and revolutions alike.
quote: the venerable and noble old man called Gregory XVI

text: The type Lord Byron made famous: proud, pale, magnetic, and haunted by some secret guilt or sorrow. Manfred and Lara are two of his heroes in this mould.
quote: Truly, a Byronic hero!

text: Riderless horses (named after the Barbary breed) raced the length of the Corso each Carnival afternoon, driven on by the crowd and by spiked weights hung on their sides.
quote: clear it for the barberi

text: One of Rome's oldest princely families, powerful since the Middle Ages, with a pope and many cardinals in its line.
quote: one of the last heiresses of the Colonnas

text: The Torlonias were Rome's great banking house, the bankers of most foreign visitors. Their fortune bought them princely titles, including the dukedom of Bracciano.
quote: Run to Torlonia, draw from him instantly four thousand piastres

text: A letter from a traveller's home bank asking bankers abroad to pay him cash up to a stated limit: the traveller's cheque of its day.
quote: take the letter of credit from my pocket-book

text: A fast, breathless ballroom dance with a hopping step, the craze of the 1830s.
quote: I was dancing the galop at Torlonia’s

text: The Via Appia, ancient Rome's great road south, begun in 312 BC. Roman law banned burial inside the city, so tombs lined the road for miles.
quote: the ancient Appian Way, and bordered with tombs

text: The Roman Campagna: the empty, rolling plain around Rome, malarial and thinly populated, the country of shepherds and bandits.
quote: the irregular and broken surface of the Campagna

text: Underground galleries on the Appian Way where early Christians buried their dead in niches cut into the walls, row above row. A columbarium is a chamber lined with such niches.
quote: waiting for him in the catacombs of St. Sebastian

text: Julius Caesar's own brisk accounts of his wars in Gaul and his civil war, classic reading for would-be commanders.
quote: Cæsar’s Commentaries

term: Never awaken me but for bad news
text: A maxim attributed to Napoleon: good news can wait until morning, while bad news needs action at once.
quote: Never awaken me but for bad news

text: Italian: 'Come up!'
quote: Salite!

text: Alejandro Aguado and James de Rothschild were the two most famous financiers in 1830s Paris, bywords for colossal wealth and stock-market speculation.
quote: the speculations of M. Aguado and M. Rothschild

term: a Huron or a native of Cochin-China
text: Stock examples of the utterly foreign: the Huron were a Native American people the French knew from Canada; Cochin-China is southern Vietnam.
quote: no more than a Huron or a native of Cochin-China

text: Prizes for virtue founded by the philanthropist Baron de Montyon and awarded each year by the French Academy to poor people of exemplary goodness. Albert is joking.
quote: to compete for the Monthyon prize

text: Corsican 'bandits' were usually men hiding in the hills after a vendetta killing, and Romantic writers admired them. The nod is to Mérimée's Corsican tale Colomba (strictly, published a couple of years after this scene).
quote: the bandits of Colomba

text: A pocket notebook of ivory or paper leaves for jotting memoranda.
quote: taking out his tablets

text: A separate small building within the grounds of a large house. Albert's gives him a bachelor's independence while living on his parents' property.
quote: occupy a pavilion at the farther side of the courtyard

text: French: the doorkeeper who lives in a lodge at the entrance of a Paris house and watches everyone who comes and goes.
quote: close to the lodge of the concierge

text: From the Arabian Nights: the robbers' cave in 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves' opens only to the password 'Open, Sesame!' Albert's private door opens to a secret knock.
quote: at the “Sesame” of Ali Baba

text: The three manly arts of a fashionable 1830s dandy. Single-stick is fencing with a wooden stick; Grisier was the most celebrated Paris fencing master.
quote: fencing, boxing, and single-stick

text: Turkish pipes: the chibouque has a long straight stem; the narghile (hookah) draws smoke through perfumed water. Oriental smoking was the height of fashion.
quote: a collection of German pipes, of chibouques

quote: you drive Don Carlos out of Spain

quote: they sent me the order of Charles III.

text: The Paris stock exchange. News that reached it early could make a speculator a fortune overnight.
quote: it had already transpired on the Bourse

text: The Chamber of Deputies, the elected lower house of parliament under King Louis-Philippe. Deputies like Danglars and journalists like Beauchamp hurry to its sittings.
quote: I must go to the Chamber

text: The great wooded park on the western edge of Paris, where fashionable people rode and drove to be seen.
quote: At the Bois de Boulogne

text: French: literally 'Plague!', a mild exclamation like 'Hang it!' or 'The deuce!'
quote: Peste!

text: Peers sat for life in the Chamber of Peers, the upper house of parliament, which met in the Luxembourg Palace. Beauchamp jokes about Danglars being 'promoted' there.
quote: send him to speak at the Luxembourg

quote: to a mésalliance

quote: I give my daughter two millions

quote: You have seven martlets on your arms

quote: witness the raising of the siege

quote: decorated with the order of the Legion of Honor

quote: you only know your dull and gloomy Faubourg Saint-Germain

text: 'Punctuality is the politeness of kings' is a saying attributed to King Louis XVIII.
quote: is the politeness of kings, according to one of your sovereigns

quote: A single portrait, signed by Léopold Robert

text: The Tuscan Order of St. Stephen allowed wealthy men to endow a 'commandery', which brought a title with it. The Count admits his title was bought this way.
quote: a commandery of St. Stephen

quote: would have greatly edified d’Hozier and Jaucourt

text: Commander of the French expedition that captured Algiers in 1830, the start of France's conquest of Algeria.
quote: under the orders of Marshal Bourmont

quote: had the elder branch remained on the throne

text: Brooding, guilt-haunted heroes of Lord Byron's poems and plays: proud aristocratic outcasts with dark secrets, wildly fashionable in the 1830s.
quote: some Manfred, some Lara, some Werner

quote: refused on the previous day seven hundred guineas

text: Smelling salts: a pungent ammonia preparation sniffed from a little bottle to revive someone who feels faint.
quote: the sharp and fragrant odor of volatile salts

text: In 1838 the avenue was grand but still semi-rural, running out to the edge of Paris between gardens and scattered mansions.
quote: as you ascend the Champs-Élysées

quote: give fifty-five thousand francs to monsieur

quote: the notary empowered to sell the country house

text: A palace in central Paris whose arcaded gardens were crowded with shops, jewellers, cafés and gaming houses.
quote: the best engraver of the Palais Royal

term: “I have been almost obliged to wait”
text: Louis XIV's famous icy rebuke ('J'ai failli attendre') to a courtier whose carriage was not instantly ready.
quote: I have been almost obliged to wait

term: signed himself in the Corsican manner
text: Making the sign of the cross in the air with the thumb, a folk gesture against evil.
quote: signed himself in the Corsican manner

quote: This is not a Corsican maquis but an English garden

quote: brooding over some old history of the vendetta

text: Monks of two very strict orders, the Carthusians and the Trappists, known for silence and penance.
quote: Turn Chartreux or Trappist

quote: only related under the seal of confession

text: Donizetti's opera Lucia di Lammermoor (1835), the great hit of the day.
quote: humming an air from Lucia

text: After Waterloo the defeated imperial army withdrew south of the River Loire and was disbanded; its soldiers made their way home through a hostile country.
quote: retired with the army beyond the Loire

quote: Three brigands, called Trestaillon, Truphemy, and Graffan

text: The long, narrow peninsula at Corsica's northern tip; Rogliano is one of its villages.
quote: the little village of Rogliano, at the extremity of Cap Corse

quote: an asylum where they receive such creatures

text: A small stylised crown drawn above initials or arms, its design showing the owner's rank.
quote: surmounted by a baron’s coronet

text: A great trade fair held each July at Beaucaire on the Rhône, drawing merchants from all over Europe and the Mediterranean.
quote: the fair at Beaucaire

quote: that is, 2,500 livres of income

text: Old pre-Revolution silver coins (écus) worth six livres, roughly six francs: here, the couple's entire savings.
quote: two or three crowns of six livres each

text: The violent, cold north wind that roars down the Rhône valley, often for days at a time.
quote: It’s the mistral

text: The Cour d'assises, the court that tried serious crimes before a jury in periodic sessions.
quote: at the approaching assizes

term: the language in which Homer makes his gods converse
text: That is, Greek: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey are written in ancient Greek.
quote: that sonorous language in which Homer makes his gods converse

text: A large torch or candlestick.
quote: a rose-colored flambeau

text: A pair of eyeglasses or opera glasses held up on a handle.
quote: by means of an excellent lorgnette

text: Six million francs to be spent in one year. For scale: the Count pays his valet 1,500 francs a year, and a family could live comfortably on 25,000 a year. Orders on the treasury were government bonds payable to whoever held them.
quote: suppose we say six millions

text: A valet's wage, plus lodging, food and perks. As the Count says, it was more than many junior officers earned.
quote: You receive 1,500 francs per annum

quote: the example set you by Messrs. de Montmorency and Lafayette

text: The giants of European banking: Baron James de Rothschild in Paris, the Barings of London, and Jacques Laffitte, a Paris banker who had also been prime minister.
quote: drawn by Baring of London, upon M. Lafitte

text: A small, fast three-masted warship.
quote: into which my corvette can enter

text: Fresh horses kept ready at intervals along a road so that a traveller could change teams and keep going at full speed.
quote: constant relays of horses at ten leagues apart

text: François Boucher, 18th-century painter of frothy pastoral scenes with pretty shepherds and shepherdesses.
quote: after the style and manner of Boucher

text: The government of France from 1795 to 1799. Its taste was a showy imitation of Greek and Roman antiquity.
quote: as it was understood during the time of the Directory

text: Fashionable horse races were held on the Champ-de-Mars parade ground in Paris and at Satory near Versailles.
quote: the indifferent races at the Champ-de-Mars and Satory

term: the Italian opera is in London
text: The fashionable Paris season ran through winter and spring. In summer the Théâtre-Italien's star singers left to perform in London.
quote: the Italian opera is in London

text: A popular park and open-air ballroom at Passy, on the edge of the Bois de Boulogne.
quote: Your horses got as far as Ranelagh

text: An elegant quarter of grand town houses with large gardens on the right bank, west of the Tuileries.
quote: her residence in the Faubourg Saint-Honoré

text: Founded in Paris in 1834 to promote horse racing, it quickly became the most exclusive gentlemen's club in the city.
quote: recounted it at the Jockey Club

text: The Doctrinaires were moderate liberal politicians (Guizot was the best known) who championed constitutional monarchy under Louis-Philippe.
quote: whether the government was doctrinaire liberal, or conservative

text: For Villefort's generation: the Bourbon Restoration of 1814, Napoleon's return in 1815, the second Restoration after Waterloo, and the July Revolution of 1830. He has prospered under every regime.
quote: Four successive revolutions had built and cemented the pedestal

text: Latin, from Horace: punishment follows the criminal 'with limping foot', slowly but surely.
quote: it is the pede claudo of the ancients

text: The lex talionis, 'an eye for an eye': punishment that exactly matches the injury.
quote: that is, the law of retaliation

text: In the Book of Tobit, young Tobias travels with the archangel Raphael without knowing he is an angel. Attila the Hun was called 'the Scourge of God'.
quote: Tobias took the angel who restored him to light

term: taken by Satan into the highest mountain
text: From the temptation of Christ in the Gospels: the devil shows Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and offers them in exchange for worship.
quote: taken by Satan into the highest mountain in the earth

text: Latin legal maxim: 'not twice for the same thing', meaning no one may be tried twice for one offence. The Count jokes that, having been nearly mad once, he cannot be again.
quote: you know the axiom,—non bis in idem

text: The old word for a stroke: sudden bleeding or blockage in the brain that can leave a person paralysed.
quote: there is apoplexy—that lightning-stroke

text: From Shakespeare's The Tempest: Ariel is an airy, almost angelic spirit; Caliban a brutish, earthbound creature.
quote: like Ariel, verge on the angelic

text: The Jacobins were the most radical club of the French Revolution. The Carbonari were secret revolutionary societies, first Italian, then French in the 1820s, plotting against the Bourbon kings.
quote: the old Jacobin, the old senator, the old Carbonaro

text: A mountainous region of north-western Greece and southern Albania, then part of the Ottoman Empire, with the Pindus range at its back.
quote: that of the women of Epirus

text: Flawless white marble from the Greek island of Paros, prized by ancient sculptors.
quote: taken for Parian marble

text: The great ancient Greek lyric poet (5th century BC), whose odes celebrate youth, victory and the gods.
quote: these lines of Pindar

text: An old quarter of Paris once full of noble mansions, by now unfashionable and given over to merchants and the middle classes. Maximilian is teasing his sister.
quote: what a fashionable woman of the Marais is

text: Two Paris dailies: La Presse (1836), the first cheap mass-circulation paper, and the respectable, pro-government Journal des Débats.
quote: la Presse and les Débats

text: The École Polytechnique, France's elite school for military engineers and artillery officers, where Maximilian trained.
quote: as they say at the Polytechnic School

text: An income from investments that meant solid upper-middle-class comfort: perhaps forty to fifty times a labourer's yearly earnings, though modest beside a banker's millions.
quote: with twenty-five thousand francs a year

text: In Ovid's story, two young Babylonians whose parents forbid their love whisper to each other through a crack in a garden wall. Shakespeare spoofs it in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
A twist on the proverb 'Man proposes, God disposes', from Thomas à Kempis.
quote: though “man proposes,” yet “money disposes.”

text: The loose smock worn by French working men; a gentleman in one was disguised as a labourer.
quote: dressed in a common gray blouse and velvet cap

text: Lucerne, or alfalfa: a clover-like crop grown for animal fodder.
quote: a scanty crop of lucern

text: Among the well-to-do, fathers chose their children's spouses for family and financial reasons. Under the Civil Code a woman under twenty-one could not marry without parental consent.
quote: from his will there was no appeal

text: 'Chair à canon', cannon fodder: a phrase popularly attributed to Napoleon's view of his conscripts.
quote: he called them ‘food for cannon,’ which was precisely

text: Old families whose nobility went back to medieval knights ('the lance') versus the new titles and fortunes won in Napoleon's wars. By the 1830s the two had begun to intermarry.
quote: with the nobility of the cannon

text: A notorious slow poison, probably arsenic-based, sold to would-be widows in 17th-century Italy and named after the woman said to have made it.
quote: the famous aqua Tofana

text: A Catholic feast in late spring, celebrated in Italy with flower-strewn streets and processions.
quote: on Corpus Christi Day

text: King of Pontus (died 63 BC), said to have made himself immune to poison by taking small doses daily. Edward is reciting his Latin school text, the biographer Cornelius Nepos.
quote: Mithridates, rex Ponticus

text: Brucine is a bitter poison closely related to strychnine; 'false angostura' is the bark of the plant that yields it, once passed off as a medicinal bark.
quote: Brucine is extracted from the false angostura

text: The caliph of Baghdad and his vizier, who roam the city in disguise in many Arabian Nights tales.
quote: are really Haroun-al-Raschids and Giaffars

text: Antoine-François Desrues, a notorious Paris poisoner executed in 1777.
quote: Desrues was, however, I must confess, more skilful

text: The demon in Lesage's novel The Devil on Two Sticks, who lifts the roofs off houses to show a student the secret lives inside.
quote: of whom Asmodeus, if you were holding on

text: Leading French physiologists of the day, famous for their experiments on animals.
quote: against M. Magendie or M. Flourens

text: A famous moral puzzle: if you could become rich by killing an unknown mandarin in China with a mere wish, would you? It was often attributed to Rousseau, though it is not found in his works.
quote: the mandarin who is killed five hundred leagues off

text: The Académie Royale de Musique: the official name of the Paris Opéra, home of grand opera and ballet.
quote: to escort to the Académie a Greek princess

text: Meyerbeer's grand opera (1831), the sensation of the age, about a knight whose father Bertram is secretly a demon. The bass Levasseur created the role of Bertram.
quote: made his reappearance in the character of Bertram

text: A box at the Opéra rented jointly by a group of fashionable young men, who came and went as they pleased.
quote: his right of entry into the omnibus box

text: A respectable woman could not appear at the opera with only her daughter; a gentleman had to accompany them.
quote: impossible for her to go alone with Eugénie to the opera

text: The parterre: the floor of the theatre behind the orchestra, filled with ordinary paying spectators, who could be noisy critics.
quote: cried the pit in chorus

text: In Greek myth the hunter Actaeon saw the virgin goddess Diana bathing; she turned him into a stag and his own hounds tore him apart.
quote: bring on me the fate of Actæon

term: the coronation of the queen of England
text: Queen Victoria was crowned on 28 June 1838. The theft of the jewels of Mademoiselle Mars, the great comic actress, was another real-life sensation Albert lumps in with it.
quote: the coronation of the queen of England took place

text: An 18th-century adventurer and self-styled magician who claimed secret, even supernatural, knowledge.
quote: Being no disciple of Cagliostro

text: Plato reportedly defined man as a 'featherless biped'; the Cynic philosopher Diogenes mocked this by holding up a plucked chicken.
quote: featherless bipeds, to quote the late Diogenes

text: Ali Pasha of Tepelenë (c.1740–1822), an Albanian warlord who ruled Epirus from Yanina (Ioannina) almost as an independent prince, defying the Ottoman sultan until the sultan's forces brought him down.
quote: at the court of Ali Tepelini

text: A long hooded cloak of the kind worn in North Africa and the East.
quote: wrapping herself in her burnouse of white cashmere

text: The army department that bought food and supplies. Contractors and officials in it often grew rich, honestly or otherwise.
quote: M. Danglars in the commissariat department

text: Two heroes of medieval French chivalry: Bayard, 'the knight without fear and without reproach', and Du Guesclin, famous for his courage and his lack of money.
quote: the integrity of a Bayard united to the poverty of a Duguesclin

text: Bonds linked to the huge indemnity Haiti was forced to pay France in 1825 in return for recognition of its independence. They were notoriously volatile, a favourite for gambling.
quote: the last rise in Haiti bonds

term: Denaro e santità, metà della metà
text: Italian: 'Money and holiness: half of half' — believe only a quarter of what you hear about anyone's wealth or virtue.
quote: Denaro e santità

text: Card games popular in Paris drawing rooms. Écarté was a fast two-player game for high stakes.
quote: Haitians are the écarté of French stock-jobbing

quote: some telegraphic despatch, of which you alone are in possession

text: Henri IV's mistress was Gabrielle d'Estrées, and his bronze statue stands on the Pont-Neuf. Albert's joke is a piece of obviously absurd 'news' that the statue went visiting.
quote: Henri IV. was seen yesterday at Gabrielle’s

text: A seaside resort on the Normandy coast, made fashionable by King Louis-Philippe's family, who stayed nearby at the château of Eu.
quote: we shall be at Tréport
